fields.meta_title: Free Interior Design Questionnaire Builder | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build an interior design questionnaire that turns each client's answers into the first draft of the design plan. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build an Interior Design Questionnaire That Shapes the Plan
fields.hero_description: Describe your clients and the projects you take on. Emergent builds the interior design questionnaire and saves every household's answers in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Happens to a Client's Answers
fields.features_subheading: Every answer a client gives should change something in the design. These six pieces carry each one into the project file.
fields.feature_1:
Room-by-room photo uploads

Ask clients to upload a few phone photos of each room in scope, with rough room sizes. Every photo is saved next to that room's answers, ready for the first site visit.
fields.feature_2:
Style picks from pairs of rooms

Show two rooms side by side and ask which feels closer to home. Picking is easier than naming a style, and a client who chooses six warm, rustic rooms has told you plenty.
fields.feature_3:
Keep or replace, piece by piece

List the main furniture in each room and have the client mark every piece keep or replace. The replace list becomes your first sourcing sheet, grouped by room for budgeting.
fields.feature_4:
Budget brackets set against your minimum

Offer budget brackets instead of an open box, with one bracket below the minimum you take on. Each bracket leads to its own next step, such as a booking link or an e-design offer.
fields.feature_5:
Reminders for half-finished answers

Send a reminder email when a questionnaire is left half done for three days. It names the rooms still missing answers and stops the moment the client finally submits the form.
fields.feature_6:
The questionnaire app, exported to GitHub

Export the full codebase to your GitHub on paid plans at any point. A developer can add a client portal or a proposal page later, and every past answer stays in the same database.

fields.tab_content_1:
Six fabrics changed after one answer about the dogs

Mara Quinn designs family homes, and her questionnaire opens with who lives in the house. The Hollis family lists two dogs and a toddler. Six upholstered pieces planned for the family room and den switch to performance fabric before Mara sources a single swatch.
fields.tab_content_2:
An office sized to its busiest day, not its payroll

Northline Workplace is fitting out a new floor for Corvid Analytics, which has 48 people on staff. The questionnaire asks how many come in on the busiest day of the week. The office manager answers 34. The desk plan starts at 34 desks, 14 fewer than the headcount.
fields.tab_content_3:
Budget answers that sort consultation leads from e-design

Sable Room Studio takes on full-service projects of $40,000 or more. Its questionnaire asks every inquiry to pick a budget bracket. Three inquiries arrived this week. The two at or above the minimum get a link to book a consultation, and the one under $40,000 gets the studio's e-design package by email.
fields.tab_content_4:
Eight guests and three bedrooms make a five-bed plan

Lark Cottage sleeps eight guests, and its host hired Tidewell Design to furnish it. The questionnaire asks how many guests the listing should sleep and how many bedrooms there are. The answers become a bed plan: a king, a queen, two twins, and a queen sofa bed in the den.

fields.howto_title: How to Write an Interior Design Questionnaire
fields.howto_description: Start from the decisions the first meeting has to make, then write only the questions that feed them.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List what the first meeting needs
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Ask who lives in the home
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Show styles instead of naming them
fields.howto_step_1_des: List the decisions you need settled before a first design meeting: the rooms in scope, the budget bracket, the completion date, and who signs off. Every question should feed one of them. Anything else can wait for the meeting itself.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Ask how many people and pets share the space, and how each room gets used on a normal weekday. Put those questions near the top of the form, because the answers decide fabric and storage long before style comes up.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask for a few photos of every room on the list and a rough width and length. Phone photos are enough at this stage. They show awkward windows and doorways before you walk in, and they fill gaps in a client's descriptions.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Most clients cannot name a style, but they can pick between two rooms. Show pairs of images and ask which feels closer, then add a free-text box for anything they already dislike, such as brass fixtures or dark floors.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Offer three or four brackets in place of a blank amount field, with the lowest one set below your minimum. A client who picks it can be offered e-design or a single consultation instead of a full-service proposal that will not fit.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Ask what stays and what goes
fields.howto_step_6_des: List the main pieces in each room and ask the client to mark each one keep or replace. The replace list starts your sourcing, and the keep list tells you which finishes and colors the new pieces have to live with.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Fill it in yourself on a phone
fields.howto_step_7_des: Open the link on a phone and answer as a busy client would, skipping every optional field and uploading one blurry photo. Check that each answer lands where it should, then send the questionnaire with the date you need it back.

plan.angle: The live top 10 is designers' own questionnaires (HiLo Decor's web form, a Divine Elements of Design PDF), template posts from DesignFiles and Mydoma, an Etsy Canva template, a Scribd copy and two blog guides. Every one is a list of questions that ends at the last page. This page treats the questionnaire as the first working file of the project: a household's pets and children mark which upholstery needs performance fabric, an office's busiest-day count sets the desk plan, a budget answer decides whether a lead gets a consultation or an e-design offer, and a rental's guest count becomes a bed plan. The FAQ follows the related searches on templates, PDF and free versions, office and home versions, checklists and consultation templates.
tab_stories: A residential designer's questionnaire asks who lives in the home, the Hollis family lists two dogs and a four-year-old, and the six upholstered pieces planned for the family room and den are marked for performance fabric before sourcing starts.
A workplace designer fitting out a 48-person analytics firm asks how many people are in on the busiest day, the answer is 34, and the desk plan starts at 34 desks instead of 48.

A full-service studio with a $40,000 minimum asks every new inquiry for a budget bracket, and the one inquiry this week under that minimum gets the studio's e-design package instead of a consultation slot.

A designer furnishing vacation rentals asks how many guests a cottage should sleep, the host answers eight across three bedrooms, and the answers become a bed plan with a king, a queen, two twins and a queen sofa bed.
